\chapter{Por --- And Three Phrases You Already Owned}
\label{ch:por}
\hlchaptermodality{154}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use por for a cause, a route or an exchange, and say what por favor literally means.}

Complete ES-C51-por: say what por favor literally means and name the English word that is the per inside por.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[por]{por — and you already know three of these}

\label{lesson:ES-C51-por}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}please.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Por favor}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}why.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{¿Por qué?}) Say \textquotedblleft{}because.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Porque}.) You have been carrying this word since your first page and nobody has told you what it means.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the arrow points back, or through}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{por} — \emph{for}, when something is the \textbf{cause}, the \textbf{route}, or what is given \textbf{in exchange}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Gracias \textbf{por} la comida.} — Thanks \textbf{for} the meal. \emph{(the cause)} \emph{\textbf{Por} ti.} — Because of you. \emph{(the cause)}
\end{quote}

Where \emph{para} pointed forward at a target, \emph{por} points \textbf{back at a reason} or \textbf{through a middle} — what something came through, not what it heads toward.

Now look again at the three phrases you already own:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{\textbf{por favor}} — literally \emph{by way of a favour}. You are not aiming at a favour; you are asking \textbf{through} one.
  \item \emph{\textbf{¿por qué?}} — literally \emph{through what?} — that is, \textbf{caused by what?}
  \item \emph{\textbf{porque}} — the same two words fused into an answer: \emph{because}.
\end{itemize}

Three of your oldest phrases turn out to be the same preposition, doing exactly what this chapter says it does. You knew \emph{por} before you knew \emph{hola} meant anything.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Por} is two Latin words run together: \textbf{pro} (\textquotedblleft{}in front of, on behalf of\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{per} (\textquotedblleft{}through\textquotedblright{}).

The \emph{per} half is still alive and unchanged in English, in the least poetic corner of the language:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{per hour}, \textbf{per person}, \textbf{per cent} — \emph{cent} being \emph{hundred}, so literally \textbf{through each hundred}.
  \item \textbf{percolate}, \textbf{permeate}, \textbf{perforate} — all piercing \emph{through}.
\end{itemize}

English kept \emph{per} meaning \textquotedblleft{}through\textquotedblright{} and Spanish kept it inside \emph{por}. Saying \emph{por favor}, you are using the same word as \emph{miles per hour}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}por favor\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}¿por qué?\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}porque\textquotedblright{} — three old friends, one word
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Gracias por la comida\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which direction does \emph{por} point? (\textbf{Back at a cause}, or \textbf{through} something.) What is \emph{por favor} literally? (\textbf{By way of a favour}.) Which English word is the \emph{per} inside it? (\emph{\textbf{Per}}, as in \emph{per hour}.) Next: the two side by side.
\end{tcolorbox}
